body:
Gold, Salt and the Sahara (lesson): The south (Bambuk, Bure) had gold but little salt, and people in a hot climate needed salt in their diet and to preserve food; the Sahara (Taghaza) had salt but no gold or farmland; North African traders wanted gold. Camels made the two-month desert crossing possible. Ghana's kings taxed salt coming in and gold going out and kept the largest nuggets; Mali controlled the gold fields and the Niger River trading cities. Either kingdom is fine.

Mali Through Travelers' Eyes (assignment):
Sourcing 1. Source A: al-Umari, an official in Cairo, writing about 1337-1338 from what Cairo officials and merchants remembered of Mansa Musa's 1324 visit; he never went to Mali. Source B: Ibn Battuta, a scholar and judge from Tangier, who visited Mali in 1352-1353 and dictated his account to Ibn Juzayy, who wrote it down in 1355.
Sourcing 2. Both were Muslim scholars from North Africa or Egypt: they praised Mali's Islamic practice and order, and Ibn Battuta judged some local customs by his own strict standards; al-Umari's informants were impressed by gold, the thing visitors noticed most.
Context 1. Cairo lay on the route to Mecca for the hajj; Mansa Musa spent and gave so much gold that its value in Cairo fell for years.
Context 2. Oral tradition preserves Mali's own view of its history, its founders (Sundiata), family lines and values; written sources by outsiders may miss these.
Claim. Model: The sources show that Mali was extremely wealthy and well governed in the 1300s. Al-Umari's informants said so much gold came into Cairo that its value fell. Ibn Battuta wrote that "there is complete safety in their country" and that a dead merchant's goods were kept safe for his heir, which shows strong laws and order that protected trade. Left out: the lives of farmers, miners and enslaved people, women's own views, and Mali's own oral history.

What Made Mali Powerful? (assessment): Any of the three causes can earn full credit. Gold: control of the gold fields; gold so plentiful its value fell in Cairo. Trade routes: Mali's cities linked desert caravans with the Niger River; taxes on trade. Rulers' choices: Ibn Battuta's account of safety and justice made trade safe; Mansa Musa brought back scholars and an architect, and Timbuktu became a center of learning. A strong answer explains how causes connect (order kept the routes safe, which kept gold flowing).

Scoring tip: for the limits criterion, Proficient names a group or view missing from the sources; Advanced explains why those authors would miss it (they were outsiders, men, scholars, or relied on others' memories). Do not accept the claim that Mali had no history before outsiders wrote about it.
title: Answer key: West African Empires
